objects.text_str: French League
history\default.hsr
Having given the World Cup and European
Championships to the sport, it is in many
respects surprising that the reputation of
French domestic football remains below that
of other European countries such as
England, Spain and Italy, with the sport at
club level seemingly failing to completely
capture the imagination of the French public.
In the years since the formation of the
Fédération Française de Football (FFF), that
comparatively low level of public support for
the domestic game has seen the sport
develop at a slower rate than the other
major footballing countries on the continent
and it remains to be seen whether or not the
national side winning the 1998 World Cup
will stimulate growth at club level.
Whilst the sport was developing a pace in the
Britain and other parts of northern Europe in
the second half of the twentieth century, the
sport in France found itself competing for
popularity with rugby.  It was out of the
rugby clubs that the earliest French club sides
in fact were formed, with the first such
football team established in the north of the
country by the Le Havre Athletic Club in
The first truly national league within the
country did not come into being until 1932
and the legislating by the FFF of
professionalism in the sport.  Prior to that
date, the French Cup had existed as the only
national competition in the country.  The now
defunct Olympique Lille became the first
winners of the championship and in the years
up to the outbreak of war, the competition
was shared out between a further four clubs.
Both FC Sete and FC Sochaux lifted the
trophy on two occasions, whilst the more
familiar names of Olympique Marseilles and
Racing Club of Paris each picked up a title
apiece.
The end of the war saw the fledgling league
picking up credibility, as with the introduction
of the European club competitions, French
sides started showing their mettle on a wider
stage.  Stade de Reims were the first such club
to do so as they reached the finals of the
European Cup in both 1956 and 1959, only
to have the misfortune of meeting the
dominant Real Madrid team of the era, with
Olympique Nice also progressing through into
the last eight in both 1957 and 1960.
However, despite the early promise that was
shown by Reims and, to a lesser extent, Nice,
the country would have to wait until the
mid-1990s before one of its clubs actually
went on to lift one of the trophies.  Indeed
such was the comparative retardation of the
development of French club football that it
was not until 1976 that a French club
eventually managed to reach another final
with St. Etienne's defeat at the hands of
Bayern Munich in 1976.
During that period the league did not
develop in tandem with their competitions of
their neighbouring countries namely
Germany, Italy or Spain and, as a
consequence, a large number of the country's
best players took little time to move to the
more successful clubs abroad.  One of the
main reasons for this was a French law passed
at the turn of the century that forbid any club
from paying significant transfer fees and from
making any form of profit from the club.  Not
the most helpful of laws when one considers
the financial power of the major club sides
outside of the country.
In 1993, the fortunes of French football
appeared to be on the up as Olympique
Marseilles became the first club from the
country to win a European trophy, when
they defeated Milan in the finals of the
European Cup.  For the previous five
seasons, Marseilles had collected successive
French league titles under the ownership of
Bernard Tapie to become the most dominant
side in French football since the days of St.
Etienne in the late 1960s and mid-70s.
However, what should have been French
football's finest hour, instead turned into one
of its worst, as the achievements of Marseilles
were devalued in the unveiling of a bribery
scandal involving the club.  It was revealed
that Tapie, in their last match before the
European final, had paid Valenciennes to
take it easy in their match with Marseilles, in
the game that sealed the side's fifth title.  As a
consequence of the findings, Marseilles were
stripped of their league and European titles,
as well as being relegated to the Second
Division of French football, with Tapie and a
number of others jailed for their part in the
scandal.  The scandal shook the French game
to the core, which only with the passing of
time can it ever hope to recover.
Five years on the future of French football,
particularly with the increase in TV money
flowing into the game, together with the
national side's success in the 1998 World
Cup, looks comparatively healthy and well on
its way to forgetting about the Marseilles
affair.  However, it remains to be seen
whether the comparatively low attendances
at league matches will increase as a result of
the World Cup triumph, which would in turn
slowly bring in much needed revenue to the
clubs, or whether the French will slowly fall
back into their somewhat indifferent attitude
to club football.
